analysis.one_liner: Makes the lower individual tax rates on capital gains and dividends permanent.
analysis.headline: A bill to permanently extend the 2003 capital gains and dividend tax cuts, backed by 122 House Republicans, never received a vote: it sat in the Ways and Means Committee until Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2003 tax law cut the tax rates on capital gains (profits from selling investments) and on stock dividends, but those cuts were written to expire after 2008. This bill would remove that expiration date and make the lower rates permanent. It was introduced by Rep. Eric Cantor with 122 Republican cosponsors and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that pay taxes on capital gains and stock dividends. Ownership of taxable capital gains and dividend income is heavily concentrated among the wealthiest households, so a permanent extension of the lower rates would deliver most of its benefit to them. The financial services industry — brokerages, mutual funds, and asset managers — also benefits because lower rates on investment income encourage more investing and trading through those channels.

how_it_helps.text: Makes the reduced capital gains tax rates from the 2003 Jobs and Growth Tax Relief Reconciliation Act permanent by removing their scheduled expiration.
The bill's title and text extend the permanence to individual income tax rates for both capital gains and dividends.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury bears the cost of forgoing the revenue that would have been raised after 2008 when the lower rates were scheduled to expire. That lost revenue must be made up through larger deficits, future tax increases elsewhere, or reduced government spending.

drawbacks.text: Making the cuts permanent removes the revenue the government would have collected once the rates were scheduled to expire after 2008, adding to deficits or forcing other taxes or spending to make up the difference.
Because capital gains and dividend income is concentrated among the highest-income households, the bill's benefits flow overwhelmingly to that group rather than to working households generally.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a permanent tax benefit aimed at a narrow, well-off group of investors at the price of permanent federal revenue loss. Even supporters of the lower rates had reason to prefer a different vehicle: Congress ultimately handled the issue through shorter extensions rather than this permanent fix, and this bill never even reached a committee vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Eric Cantor introduced the bill on February 15, 2005, joined by eight original cosponsors including Reps. Paul Ryan, Dave Camp, and Jim McCrery.
The bill attracted 122 cosponsors, all of them Republicans.

The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction, and the action history shows no further action — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one lost anything they already had, since the lower rates remained law through their scheduled 2008 expiration regardless. Relative to the bill, the federal treasury and future taxpayers came out ahead by avoiding the cost of making the cuts permanent; investors with large gains and dividends lost only the prospect of a permanent guarantee.

for.name: Eric Cantor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the capital gains and dividend rate cuts permanent.

for.name: Paul Ryan, Jim McCrery, Dave Camp, Phil English, Tom Reynolds, Jerry Lewis, Wally Herger, and Michael McCaul
for.role: Original cosponsors; several were Ways and Means Committee members
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Republican-controlled in the 109th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 122 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never advanced far enough to produce a floor vote or recorded opposition.

industries.note: The bill would permanently lock in lower tax rates on capital gains and dividends, income streams concentrated among the wealthiest households. The cost of that permanent benefit would be borne through foregone federal revenue that other taxpayers must eventually cover.

industries.industry: Financial services (brokerages, mutual funds, asset managers)
industries.note: Lower permanent rates on investment income encourage more investing and trading, which runs through financial firms as fees and assets under management. The benefit to the industry is indirect and follows from the rate cut rather than a direct subsidy.
